summary: Deep technical sync focused on artifact delivery for an air-gapped deployment and runtime tuning knobs (KV cache, batching, quantization). transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-08-20 16:00 PT | Duration: 62m
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Lina (Redwood SE), Omar (Redwood Support), Marco (Tempest MLOps), Anika (Infra), Ethan (Security), Priya (SRE)

[00:00] Jordan: Okay, thanks everyone for joining. quick agenda — artifact packaging and transfer for air-gap, offline license, driver matrix, and then a short perf tuning and kv cache discussion. does that align?
[00:20] Marco: Yep that's perfect. We mostly want to make sure we can install without outbound access and hit our p95 SLOs.
[00:35] Lina: Great, I'll kick off with the artifact story — so for air-gapped installs we deliver a signed tarball that contains container images (OCI layout), our runtime binaries, model wheel, and a license blob. The tarball is PGP-signed and we include SHA256 checksums for each image and artifact.
[00:55] Anika: Quick Q — how big are we talking? Our transfer pipeline is a jumpbox with 1Gbps and we prefer smaller chunks so rsync is easier.
[01:10] Lina: Typical full stack for a medium LLM is around 40-120GB depending on model size and quantization artifacts. We recommend splitting into parts and using resumable transfer; we provide a manifest with chunking instructions.
[01:28] Ethan: From security side we need to know how the license blob is generated and validated. Is there a central call-home or is validation fully offline?
[01:45] Jordan: It's fully offline for Tempest's plan — we generate a signed license blob that the local license agent validates using embedded public keys. No outbound to Redwood required. For long-running installs we offer an optional periodic CSR flow if customers want pro-rated revocation checks but that's separate.
[02:05] Priya: Can that license blob tie to host IDs? we need it to be tied to hardware ids and an expiration.
[02:15] Jordan: Yes we bind to a host fingerprint and optional HSM-stored keys. We'll include the host manifest format in the checklist.
[02:28] Marco: About GPU drivers — our cluster is mixed nvidia 40 series and A100s. we run centos 8. what driver versions are required? we had issues with 525 vs 530 previously.
[02:45] Lina: Right, the runtime is sensitive to driver/NCCL/CUDA combos. For A100 we validate against NVIDIA driver 515+ with CUDA 11.7 and NCCL 2.12. For 40-series we recommend 525+ and CUDA 12.1 for best cuBLAS kernels. We'll provide a compatibility matrix.
[03:05] Omar: small note — sometimes our packaging uses containerd and CRI-O — we test both but there are known quirks with snapshotters and mmap flags, so we include a container runtime compatibility doc.
[03:28] Anika: Do you require nvhpc or the NVIDIA driver only? we run modules and can't install the whole toolkit easily.
[03:38] Lina: Only the driver stack plus the CUDA runtime libraries in the artifact images. We ship our own libcudart in the containers, so host can avoid full toolkit installs in some configurations, but driver kernel module must match.
[03:55] Marco: What about MIG/reservation? we carve entire GPUs usually. any special notes?
[04:05] Lina: Redwood runtime supports whole-GPU provisioning. MIG not fully supported for all models yet — we list specific models that can run on MIG slices in the matrix. For initial rollout we suggest whole-GPU for predictable throughput.
[04:20] [Brief crosstalk, someone drops a file path]
[04:35] Jordan: On the perf front — quick baseline numbers: for model X (70B fp16) we see ~120 tokens/sec p50 on an A100 with our optimized kernels and batching; p95 latency around 180-250ms depending on seq length and prompt prefixes. With INT8/q4_0-like quantization that throughput can increase 1.7-2.5x depending on model and quality tradeoffs.
[04:58] Marco: 120 tokens/sec p50 — is that with KV cache warm? and what's the batch/window config?
[05:10] Lina: Those numbers assume a warmed KV cache and batching window tuned to 6-12ms micro-batch (continuous batching). We often do a two-tier batching: small low-latency window for interactive (1-4 requests) and a high-throughput mode for async workloads.
[05:28] Priya: Explain the KV cache persistence — if a node restarts, do we lose cache and does that spike latency?
[05:40] Omar: Good Q — by default KV cache is in-memory but we have optional snapshotting to a local fast NVMe store; snapshot/restore on restart reduces warm-up to milliseconds depending on model size. However, snapshotting requires an FS with good IOPS.
[05:58] Ethan: How large are snapshots? for a 70B model?
[06:08] Lina: Rough rule: full attention KV for long context can be tens of GBs — e.g. a warm KV for 70B at 4k context could be ~40-80GB. We compress and shingle to reduce size, but you should expect large snapshots.
[06:30] Marco: That matters for our islanded nodes — NVMe is limited on a few racks.
[06:40] Jordan: We'll note that in the checklist — recommended local SSD sizes and IOPS.
[06:50] Anika: On quantization — which modes do you support? our compliance team is worried about hallucination/regression when going to INT8.
[07:02] Lina: We support FP16, BF16, INT8-like post-training quantization, and some of our Q4_K_M variants for friendly speed/quality tradeoffs. We always recommend running evals on a masked-prod prompt set; Redwood Optimize suggests model/quant combo per workload. For safety-critical outputs, stay FP16 or controlled QAT.
[07:28] Marco: For the artifact we should include quantized model artifacts separately?
[07:35] Lina: Yes — artifacts include base fp16 model + recommended quantized variants. Each variant gets its own checksum entry in the manifest.
[07:48] [08:00] Ethan: Security — what's inside the runtime regarding telemetry? We need audit logs only, no heuristic telemetry to leave the cluster.
[08:10] Jordan: By default telemetry is off in air-gapped mode. We provide a telemetry toggle and a separate collection agent that writes structured logs to local storage and can be shipped manually if you opt in. Audit logs for access and API keys are local.
[08:28] Priya: SSO/SSO integration when we later connect the control plane? we need SAML and SCIM.
[08:37] Jordan: Private control plane supports SAML SSO and SCIM via an AD connector; for truly air-gapped installs you manage auth locally and we show the config for the local admin portal.
[08:48] Marco: Back to performance tuning — what's your recommendation for batching params to balance p95 latency and cost?
[09:00] Lina: Start with conservative micro-batching windows (6-12ms) for interactive endpoints and tune up to 25-50ms for higher throughput. Also enable prefix caching where applicable. We have a small perf script that runs kv-warm and sweeps batch/window sizes — Lina will share.
[09:20] Anika: Can we run that script in our staging lab without the full stack?
[09:28] Omar: Yes, we provide a lightweight runtime image that exercises only the kernel hot paths and KV plumbing; it doesn't require the model artifacts and is under 2GB. Good for verifying driver/NCCL/CUDA behavior.
[09:45] Marco: There's been noise around NCCL 2.14 and RDMA; we use Mellanox and want to know if variants need specific flags.
[09:55] Lina: We test with OFED and recent NCCL releases. For RDMA we recommend libibverbs and tuned MTU settings; we'll include an RNIC tuning doc.
[10:10] Priya: Do you support CPU-only fallback for small models? sometimes we want a low-cost fallback on nodes without GPUs.
[10:20] Lina: Yes, we ship CPU kernels but performance is much lower. We suggest dedicated small CPU endpoints for trivial embedding tasks, not for heavy generation.
[10:32] Jordan: Quick perf note — for demos we usually show tokens/sec and p95 latency across three modes: warmed-KV FP16, warmed-KV INT8, and cold-start FP16. We'll share sample numbers and plots.
[10:45] Marco: On the install day — what's the preferred dry-run sequence?
[10:52] Lina: Plan: 1) validate GPU/driver matrix using lightweight runtime tool, 2) import images into airgap registry, 3) staging install with a single node, run perf script and KV snapshot, 4) expand to a small pool and run scaled traffic test.
[11:10] Anika: For registry import — we need an index of images and manifest. do you support OCI layout and cri-o imports?
[11:20] Omar: Yes OCI layout supported. We include 'skopeo copy' commands and an import script tailored for containerd and CRI-O. We also supply a signed manifest and instructions for 'ctr images import'.
[11:35] Ethan: Regarding licensing — will you provide a test license with a shorter TTL for the dry-run?
[11:45] Jordan: Yes we can provide a 7-day test license blob for staging. Production licenses will be host-bound and time-limited.
[11:55] Marco: Any gotchas with driver stack and kernel versions? we run some older kernels 5.4 on centos variants.
[12:05] Lina: We recommend 5.10+ for full driver compatibility; older kernels sometimes require backported patches. We'll include a kernel compatibility table.
[12:20] Anika: Are there known issues with systemd cgroups v2?
[12:28] Omar: runtime supports cgroup v2 but some older OCI runtimes had issues. Our test matrix includes both; we'll flag any known edge cases.
[12:40] Jordan: All right, let's do a quick recap of next steps — Jordan to share artifact checklist and signed tarball sample, Lina to send perf script and driver matrix, Anika to send GPU inventory and constraints, Tempest team to run validation and report results.
[12:58] Marco: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[13:05] Jordan: Thanks — we'll follow up in the ticket with links.

End of transcript.
